claims.source: Interestingly, 100% of mice infected with the A22R variant resolved their infections over the 4 week experiment, with half of the mice (10/20) exhibiting sterile urines by 10 dpi compared to just 15% (3/20) of mice infected with the WT strain at the same time point (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Single strain infection experiments in C3H/HeN mice over 28 days with longitudinal urinalysis.

claims.claim: Two FimA variants (A22R and D114R) significantly altered the ability of UTI89 to form IBCs at 6 hr post infection.
claims.source: Accordingly, we found that two fimA variants (A22R and D114R) significantly altered the ability of UTI89 to form IBCs at 6 hr post infection (hpi) (Figure 5G), with 8/10 mice infected with the D114R variant forming <15 IBCs.
claims.evidence: IBC enumeration in bladder wholemounts at 6 hpi.

claims.claim: 70% of mice infected with the A22R variant formed no IBCs at 6 hpi and the other 30% formed three or less.
claims.source: Even more strikingly, 70% of mice infected with the A22R variant formed no IBCs at 6 hpi and the other 30% formed three or less.
claims.evidence: IBC enumeration in bladder wholemounts at 6 hpi.

claims.claim: Wild-type and P132R strains formed between 50–100 IBCs on average by 6 hpi.
claims.source: This is in stark contrast to WT and P132R strains, which formed between 50–100 IBCs on average by 6hpi.
claims.evidence: IBC enumeration in bladder wholemounts at 6 hpi.

claims.claim: The A22R mutant was severely attenuated in its ability to invade into bladder cells starting as early as 1 hr post infection.
claims.source: Interestingly, the A22R mutant was severely attenuated in its ability to invade into bladder cells starting as early as 1 hr post infection (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: Bacterial invasion assays at 1, 3, and 6 hr post infection.

claims.claim: Strains producing FimA variants D62R, D114R, and A22R showed lower levels of intestinal colonization (by up to 2 logs) compared to wild-type.
claims.source: We found that strains producing FimAUTI89 variants D62R, D114R, and A22R showed lower levels of intestinal colonization (by up to 2 logs) in the feces, cecum, and colon of mice compared to those colonized by WT fimA (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Intestinal colonization experiments in streptomycin-treated C3H/HeN mice at 7 days post colonization.

claims.claim: The 2-log decrease in intestinal colonization by FimA mutants mirrors the defect observed in UTI89Δfim or UTI89ΔfimH strains.
claims.source: This 2-log decrease mirrors the defect observed in UTI89Δfim or UTI89ΔfimH strains, suggesting that these mutations prevent type 1 pilus-dependent gut colonization in UTI89 (Spaulding et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Comparison with previously published data on fim deletion mutants cited from Spaulding et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Type 1 pili are critical virulence factors in uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC).
claims.source: Arguably, the best-studied CUP pili are those encoded by uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC), which is the causative agent of the majority of urinary tract infections (UTIs).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge about UPEC pathogenesis discussed in the Introduction.

claims.claim: Type 1 pili facilitate bacterial colonization and subsequent invasion into epithelial cells lining the bladder lumen.
claims.source: Upon entering the bladder, type 1 pili facilitate bacterial colonization and subsequent invasion into epithelial cells lining the bladder lumen (Mulvey et al., 1998; Martinez et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies by Mulvey et al., 1998 and Martinez et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Type 1 pili help mediate UPEC intestinal colonization.
claims.source: Recent work has revealed that type 1 pili help mediate UPEC intestinal colonization, thus promoting the establishment and/or maintenance of the UPEC reservoir in the gut that can eventually seed UTI (Spaulding et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from recent work by Spaulding et al., 2017.

claims.claim: UPEC that cannot invade the urothelium are quickly cleared from the bladder.
claims.source: UPEC that cannot invade the urothelium, like those lacking type 1 pili or its associated adhesin, FimH, are quickly cleared from the bladder, emphasizing the importance of type 1 pili mediated host-pathogen interactions on the fitness of UPEC during cystitis (Wright et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Cited from Wright et al., 2005.

claims.claim: After invading into a bladder cell, UPEC escape into the host cell cytoplasm and replicate to form biofilm-like intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs) comprised of ~10^4 cells.
claims.source: After invading into a bladder cell, UPEC escape into the host cell cytoplasm and replicate to form biofilm-like intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs) (Anderson et al., 2003; Justice et al., 2004) comprised of ~104 cells (Wright et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Cited from Anderson et al., 2003; Justice et al., 2004; and Wright et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The type 1 pilus coils into a rigid right-handed helical structure that is capable of unwinding into a flexible linear fiber.
claims.source: Once extruded to the extracellular surface, the type 1 pilus coils into a rigid right-handed helical structure that is capable of unwinding into a flexible linear fiber (Abraham et al., 1992; Jones et al., 1995; Saulino et al., 2000; Aprikian et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies: Abraham et al., 1992; Jones et al., 1995; Saulino et al., 2000; Aprikian et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The type 1 pilus is proposed to act as a 'molecular spring' to maintain adherence in the face of fluid shear forces.
claims.source: This ability to transition between a coiled, helical rod and a linear fiber has been proposed to allow the type 1 pilus to act as a 'molecular spring' to maintain adherence in the face of fluid shear forces (Zakrisson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from Zakrisson et al., 2012.

claims.claim: CUP pili are critical virulence factors in a wide range of pathogenic bacteria, including Escherichia, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Salmonella and Yersiniae genera.
claims.source: Notably, CUP pili are critical virulence factors in a wide range of pathogenic bacteria, including Escherichia, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Salmonella and Yersiniae genera (Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007).
claims.evidence: Cited from Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007.

claims.claim: 38 distinct CUP pilus types have been identified in Escherichia and Shigella genomes and plasmids.
claims.source: To date, 38 distinct CUP pilus types have been identified in Escherichia and Shigella genomes and plasmids, each of which is hypothesized to promote bacterial colonization of a distinct habitat (Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007; Wurpel et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007 and Wurpel et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Single Escherichia coli genomes carry up to 16 distinct CUP operons.
claims.source: Interestingly, single Escherichia coli genomes carry up to 16 distinct CUP operons, suggesting that the retention of an assortment of CUP pilus types by a single strain may be necessary to accommodate the complex lifecycle of E. coli (Wurpel et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from Wurpel et al., 2013.

claims.claim: UTIs affect 150 million people annually worldwide.
claims.source: UTIs affect 150 million people annually worldwide and are associated with significant morbidity and economic impact (Foxman, 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from Foxman, 2014.

claims.claim: ~25% of women suffer from recurrent UTI (rUTI).
claims.source: UTI treatment failure is common, with ~25% of woman suffering from recurrent UTI (rUTI), and is due, in part, to the increasing prevalence of drug-resistant UPEC strains (Scholes et al., 2000; Zowawi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from Scholes et al., 2000 and Zowawi et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The vast majority of sequenced E. coli strains, including nearly all sequenced UPEC clinical isolates, carry an intact copy of the type 1 pilus.
claims.source: While the types of CUP pilus operons encoded in E. coli genomes varies between different clades and individual strains, the vast majority of sequenced E. coli strains, including nearly all sequenced UPEC clinical isolates, carry an intact copy of the type 1 pilus (Wurpel et al., 2013; Schreiber et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from Wurpel et al., 2013 and Schreiber et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The majority of UPEC strains isolated from women with UTI in the USA reside in the B2 clade.
claims.source: While UPEC strains tend to be genetically heterogeneous the majority of UPEC strains isolated from women with UTI in the USA reside in the B2 clade (Schreiber et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from Schreiber et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The type 1 pilus rod is a homopolymer of ~1000 FimA subunits.
claims.source: Following this pattern, the type 1 pilus usher (FimD) and chaperone (FimC) help type 1 pili assemble into a composite pilus structure consisting of a short tip fibrillum made up of the adhesin protein (FimH) and two minor subunits (FimG and FimF) that is joined to the pilus rod, a homopolymer of ~1000 FimA subunits.
claims.evidence: Established knowledge about type 1 pilus structure discussed in the Introduction.

claims.claim: The unwinding force measured for wild-type type 1 pili in this study is similar to what has been reported in the literature.
claims.source: The unwinding force measured for WT type 1 pili in this study is similar to what has been reported in the literature (Andersson et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Comparison with previously published measurements cited from Andersson et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Replacing alanine 22 with arginine is expected to disrupt the subunit interface due to steric clashes.
claims.source: Thus, replacing a small alanine with a long arginine side chain is expected to disrupt this interface.
claims.evidence: Inference based on structural analysis showing Ala22 is tightly packed against other residues.

claims.claim: The pilus rod may act as a 'molecular spring' during mucus shedding in the gut.
claims.source: In the gut, the pilus rod may play a similar role during mucus shedding.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on the bladder findings extended to the gut environment.

claims.claim: Type 1 pili may promote UPEC colonization of the upper crypts in the gut.
claims.source: A recent study suggests that type 1 pili may promote UPEC colonization of the upper crypts (Spaulding et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from Spaulding et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The clumping phenotype caused by D62R and D114R mutations suggests these mutations may alter side-to-side interactions between different pilus rods.
claims.source: However, the clumping phenotype suggests that these mutations may alter side-to-side interactions between different pilus rods promoting pilus-pilus interactions within and between bacteria, thus inhibiting the pilus mediated interactions needed in vivo for attachment, invasion and/or IBC formation.
claims.evidence: Inference based on the observed clumping phenotype and structural location of the mutations.

claims.claim: The type 1 pilus rod may mediate colonization phenotypes through damping of shear forces or through other mechanism(s) outside of scaffold support for FimH-binding.
claims.source: Together, our data suggest that the type 1 pilus rod may mediate colonization phenotypes through damping of shear forces or through other mechanism(s) outside of scaffold support for FimH-binding.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental results.

claims.claim: A wild-type rod that could never uncoil would be susceptible to breakage by shear forces.
claims.source: This would still suggest that the mechanical properties of these rods have been 'tuned' to optimize for particular environments, as a wt rod that could never uncoil would be susceptible to breakage by the shear forces, while a rod that uncoils too easily would be unnecessarily exposed to digestion by proteases.
claims.evidence: Speculation about the evolutionary optimization of rod mechanical properties.

claims.claim: A rod that uncoils too easily would be unnecessarily exposed to digestion by proteases.
claims.source: This would still suggest that the mechanical properties of these rods have been 'tuned' to optimize for particular environments, as a wt rod that could never uncoil would be susceptible to breakage by the shear forces, while a rod that uncoils too easily would be unnecessarily exposed to digestion by proteases.
claims.evidence: Speculation about the evolutionary optimization of rod mechanical properties.

claims.claim: FimA displays patterns of episodic, divergent selection on surface exposed amino acids similar to what is seen in the flagellin protein in Salmonella.
claims.source: FimA displays patterns of episodic, divergent selection on surface exposed amino acids in a pattern that is similar, though much less robust, to what is seen in the flagellin protein in Salmonella (Li et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: Comparison with known patterns in Salmonella flagellin cited from Li et al., 1994.

claims.claim: In Salmonella, the flagellin subunits are split into several domains where the domains responsible for subunit-subunit assembly are highly conserved while the more external domains show high rates of variability.
claims.source: In Salmonella, the flagellin subunits are split into several domains where the domains responsible for subunit-subunit assembly are highly conserved while the more external domains of the protein show high rates of variability (Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005; Galkin et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Cited from Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005 and Galkin et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Flagellin is bound by Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5) resulting in the induction of the innate immune response.
claims.source: While it is known that flagellin are bound by Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5) resulting in the induction of the innate immune response (Smith and Ozinsky, 2002) and that this recognition is targeted towards conserved features of flagellin (Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005), it is currently unknown which, if any, host immune receptor are capable of recognizing the FimA rod or subunits or which structural features are targeted by the host immune system.
claims.evidence: Cited from Smith and Ozinsky, 2002 and Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005.

claims.claim: It is currently unknown which, if any, host immune receptor are capable of recognizing the FimA rod or subunits.
claims.source: While it is known that flagellin are bound by Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5) resulting in the induction of the innate immune response (Smith and Ozinsky, 2002) and that this recognition is targeted towards conserved features of flagellin (Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005), it is currently unknown which, if any, host immune receptor are capable of recognizing the FimA rod or subunits or which structural features are targeted by the host immune system.
claims.evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap in the field.

claims.claim: The bacterial clumping phenotype is associated with mutation of three codons under purifying selection and an equal number of mutations in codons with little to no evidence of selective pressure.
claims.source: For example, the bacterial clumping phenotype is associated with mutation of three codons under purifying selection, but an equal number of the mutations that resulted in clumping are in codons with little to no evidence of selective pressure.
claims.evidence: Analysis of the relationship between phenotypes and selection pressure on codons.

claims.claim: All mutations that failed to complement a fimA gene deletion were made in codons that are under very strong purifying selection or are too conserved for analysis.
claims.source: In contrast, all mutations that failed to complement a fimA gene deletion were made in codons that are under very strong purifying selection or are too conserved for analysis.
claims.evidence: Analysis of the relationship between phenotypes and selection pressure on codons.

claims.claim: The mis-assembly of the pilus is much more harmful and/or toxic to E. coli than bacterial clumping.
claims.source: Together, the difference in selection pressure suggests that the mis-assembly of the pilus is much more harmful and/or toxic to E. coli than bacterial clumping.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the differences in selection pressure associated with different phenotypes.

claims.claim: Many codons under purifying selection are involved in keeping the force needed to unwind the type 1 rod within a narrow range.
claims.source: Instead, we found that many codons under purifying selection are involved in keeping the force needed to unwind the type 1 rod within a narrow range.
claims.evidence: Integration of evolutionary analysis with optical tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: A 'weak' or 'loose' FimA rod may be just as detrimental for E. coli as having no rod at all, at least in the eyes of evolution.
claims.source: This leads to reasoning that a 'weak' or 'loose' FimA rod may be just as detrimental for E. coli as having no rod at all, at least in the eyes of evolution.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the evolutionary analysis and functional studies.

claims.claim: The mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod are essential for its functional role in mediating E. coli pathogenesis and persistence.
claims.source: In summary, by combining structural studies, force spectroscopy, genetic analysis, and relevant mouse models of UTI and gut colonization, we conclude that the mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod are essential for its functional role in mediating E. coli pathogenesis and persistence and appear to have been carefully 'tuned' by evolution.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the integration of structural, biophysical, evolutionary, and in vivo experimental data.

claims.claim: The mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod appear to have been carefully 'tuned' by evolution.
claims.source: In summary, by combining structural studies, force spectroscopy, genetic analysis, and relevant mouse models of UTI and gut colonization, we conclude that the mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod are essential for its functional role in mediating E. coli pathogenesis and persistence and appear to have been carefully 'tuned' by evolution.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the integration of structural, biophysical, evolutionary, and in vivo experimental data.

claims.claim: Type IV pili can elongate under force.
claims.source: In addition, other bacterial pili, such as T4P, which have arisen independently of CUP pili but can play similar roles in pathogenesis, can also elongate under force (Biais et al., 2010) and thus it remains an interesting question as to how the physical properties of other pili have been selected for particular environments and how these properties impact bacterial pathogenesis.
claims.evidence: Cited from Biais et al., 2010.

claims.claim: There were no ambiguities in threading the known FimA sequence through the density map.
claims.source: There were no ambiguities in threading the known FimA sequence through the density map (Supplementary file 1), even though the electron density observed on the outside of the rod is less well defined (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Statement about the model building process and quality of the cryo-EM map.

claims.claim: The first two residues and the last residue of FimA are not resolved in the density map.

claims.evidence: Statement about limitations of the cryo-EM structure.

claims.evidence: Assessment of map quality features that support the stated resolution.

claims.claim: In the type 1 pilus structure, the N-terminal donor strand of one subunit completes the β-sheet of the adjacent subunit.
claims.source: Further, in the structure we observe the N-terminal donor strand of one subunit completing the β-sheet of the adjacent subunit.
claims.evidence: Direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: FimA residues 22–33 show structural differences between the cryo-EM rod structure and previously solved crystal structures of FimA.
claims.source: Further, residues corresponding to FimABW2511322–33, which are part of the interior surface of the rod helix, show structural differences between our cryo-EM rod structure and the previously solved crystal structures of FimA (Crespo et al., 2012)(Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Comparison of the cryo-EM structure with previously published crystal structures cited from Crespo et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Within the cryo-EM rod FimA structure, residues 25–29 adopt a helical conformation.
claims.source: Within the cryo-EM rod FimA structure, residues 25–29 adopt a helical conformation and residues 30–33 form a β-strand interaction with residues 10–13 from the Nte of the next FimA subunit.
claims.evidence: Structural observation from the cryo-EM model.

claims.claim: FimA residues 30–33 form a β-strand interaction with residues 10–13 from the Nte of the next FimA subunit.
claims.source: Within the cryo-EM rod FimA structure, residues 25–29 adopt a helical conformation and residues 30–33 form a β-strand interaction with residues 10–13 from the Nte of the next FimA subunit.
claims.evidence: Structural observation from the cryo-EM model.

claims.claim: The ability of FimA residues 22–33 to adopt multiple conformations may be necessary for FimA to function as the major rod subunit.
claims.source: These residues form the center strand within the hollow helical core, and thus the ability of this region to adopt multiple conformations may be necessary in order for FimA to function as the major rod subunit.
claims.evidence: Inference based on structural observations and comparison with other FimA structures.

claims.claim: The interface between subunits N0 and N+3 is extremely important in maintaining the FimA helical rod.
claims.source: The interface between subunits N0 and N+3 is extremely important in maintaining the FimA helical rod.
claims.evidence: Statement based on structural analysis of subunit interactions.

claims.claim: Two atomic models (PDB ID: 2N2H and 2MX3) for the type 1 pilus have been generated using the same solid-state NMR data.
claims.source: Previously, two atomic models (PDB ID: 2N2H and 2MX3) for the type 1 pilus have been generated using the same solid-state NMR data (Habenstein et al., 2015), with the helical symmetries for these models shown in Supplementary file 2.
claims.evidence: Cited from Habenstein et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The overall RMSD between Cα atoms of subunit N+3 in the cryo-EM model and 2N7H is 5.7 Å.
claims.source: The overall RMSD between Cα atoms of subunit N+3 in our cryo-EM model and 2N7H is 5.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), while it is 11.0 Å with 2MX3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: The overall RMSD between Cα atoms of subunit N+3 in the cryo-EM model and 2MX3 is 11.0 Å.

claims.evidence: Structural comparison calculation between different models.

claims.claim: In the P pilus, residues 1–5 are fully ordered and make a 90° bend to form a 'staple' which involves contacts with two other subunits.

claims.evidence: Comparison with P pilus structure cited from Hospenthal et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In the type 1 pilus, the first two residues are disordered and the remaining three residues in this region project straight out of the structure and make no contacts with other subunits.

claims.evidence: Structural observation from the cryo-EM model compared with P pilus.

claims.claim: Some FimA sequences contain an additional two amino acid residues at the N-terminus of the mature protein compared to BW25113.
claims.source: Here, we found that many of the FimA sequences were comprised of 159 residues, including BW25113, while other FimA sequences, such as the one from UTI89, a prototypical UPEC isolate, contained an additional two amino acid residues at the N-terminus of the mature protein (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Sequence alignment analysis of 1,828 FimA proteins.

claims.claim: The degree of divergence between alleles of FimA is abnormally high compared to most E. coli genes.
claims.source: In general, most E. coli genes evolve slowly (Lee et al., 2012), so the degree of divergence between alleles of FimA is abnormally high.
claims.evidence: Comparison with general E. coli gene evolution cited from Lee et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The selection forces acting on the FimA protein are different from the forces acting on the rest of the fim operon.
claims.source: This suggests that the selection forces acting on the FimA protein are different from the forces acting on the rest of the fim operon.
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison of conservation levels between FimA and other fim operon components.

claims.claim: The first few amino acids of the N-terminus of the mature FimA protein have some of the highest variability throughout the entire protein.
claims.source: In particular, the first few amino acids of the N-terminus of the mature protein, disordered in our reconstruction, have some of the highest variability throughout the entire protein, suggesting that these amino acids do not play a functional role in the dynamics of unwinding in the type one pilus rod.
claims.evidence: Sequence conservation analysis combined with structural observation.

claims.claim: The N-terminal amino acids of mature FimA do not play a functional role in the dynamics of unwinding in the type one pilus rod.
claims.source: In particular, the first few amino acids of the N-terminus of the mature protein, disordered in our reconstruction, have some of the highest variability throughout the entire protein, suggesting that these amino acids do not play a functional role in the dynamics of unwinding in the type one pilus rod.
claims.evidence: Inference based on high sequence variability and disorder in the structure.

claims.claim: The conservation of residues lining the lumen might be due to the transport of some product through the ~15 Å opening.
claims.source: The conservation of residues lining the lumen might be due to the transport of some product through this opening that is ~15 Å across (the height of the triangular lumen that rotates as one travels along the pilus).
claims.evidence: Speculation about the functional reason for conservation of lumen residues.

claims.claim: Every residue in the lumen is either involved in making a subunit-subunit contact or packed tightly between residues that are making such contacts.
claims.source: More likely, however, every residue in the lumen is either involved in making a subunit-subunit contact (including the DSE contacts with the Nte from an adjacent subunit) or packed tightly between residues that are making such contacts.
claims.evidence: Structural analysis of residue positions and interactions in the lumen.

claims.claim: FimAUTI89 differs from FimABW25113 in 16 residues, with all differences lying within highly variable residues located on the exterior of the pilus rod.
claims.source: Thus, we do note that FimAUTI89 differs from our cryo-EM rod FimABW25113 sequence in 16 residues, with all of the differences lying within highly variable residues located on the exterior of the pilus rod, including two additional amino acids at the N-terminus.
claims.evidence: Sequence comparison between FimAUTI89 and FimABW25113.

claims.claim: 27 codons in fimA were too conserved to be included in evolutionary analysis.
claims.source: Here, we found that 66 codons were under purifying selection, five codons were under adaptive selection, and an additional 27 codons were too conserved to be included in analysis (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: dN/dS ratio analysis of fimA sequences.

claims.claim: 63 codons in fimA showed no evidence of statistically significant selection in either direction.
claims.source: The remaining 63 codons showed no evidence of statistically significant selection in either direction.
claims.evidence: dN/dS ratio analysis of fimA sequences.

claims.claim: Evolutionary pressures are working to conserve the identity of residues that interact within the helical rod while diversifying amino acid residues exposed to the host.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that evolutionary pressures are working to conserve the identity of residues that interact within the helical rod, while diversifying amino acid residues that are exposed to the host and susceptible to immune recognition.
claims.evidence: Inference based on the pattern of purifying selection at interfaces and adaptive selection on surface residues.

claims.claim: There is not a single variant of FimA found in all UPEC strains.
claims.source: Importantly, the fimA sequences from UPEC strains were spread through the phylogenetic tree, indicating that there was not a single variant of FimA found in all UPEC strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Phylogenetic analysis of fimA sequences from UPEC and other E. coli strains.

claims.claim: fimA is much more diverse than other parts of the type 1 machinery, owing to high rates of nucleotide polymorphisms and genetic recombination.
claims.source: Taken together, we find that fimA is much more diverse than other parts of the type 1 machinery, owing to high rates of nucleotide polymorphisms and genetic recombination, and that fimA has undergone repeated rounds of strong selective pressures that have conserved residues responsible for subunit-subunit interfaces while varying the external surface of the protein that is exposed to the host milieu.
claims.evidence: Summary of evolutionary analyses including recombination detection and selection pressure measurements.

claims.claim: fimA has undergone repeated rounds of strong selective pressures that have conserved residues responsible for subunit-subunit interfaces while varying the external surface of the protein.
claims.source: Taken together, we find that fimA is much more diverse than other parts of the type 1 machinery, owing to high rates of nucleotide polymorphisms and genetic recombination, and that fimA has undergone repeated rounds of strong selective pressures that have conserved residues responsible for subunit-subunit interfaces while varying the external surface of the protein that is exposed to the host milieu.
claims.evidence: Summary of evolutionary analyses showing patterns of selection.

claims.claim: Mutations A25R, V32R, V65R, V85R, and P145R may disrupt critical interactions with FimC or FimD or may not be able to correctly fold.

claims.evidence: Inference based on the loss of pilus assembly function and location of mutations in conserved regions.

claims.claim: Residues A25, V85 and P145 were under strong purifying selection pressure.

claims.evidence: Evolutionary analysis showing selection pressure on specific codons.

claims.claim: Codons for V32 and V65 displayed no synonymous mutations and extremely limited non-synonymous mutation rates.
claims.source: Notably, each of these residues was either under strong purifying selection pressure (A25, V85 and P145) or was too conserved for evolutionary analysis (codons for V32 and V65 displayed no synonymous mutations and extremely limited non-synonymous mutation rates), which emphasizes their importance in assembly of the type 1 pilus rod (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Evolutionary analysis showing extreme conservation of specific codons.

claims.claim: D62R and D114R mutations instigated bacterial clumping to a lesser extent than V5R, E45R, E121R and A142R.
claims.source: D62R and D114R also instigated bacterial clumping, but to a lesser extent.
claims.evidence: Observation of bacterial cultures expressing mutant FimA proteins.

claims.claim: Three substitutions (E45R, E121R and A142R) that caused clumping are found in residues with relatively high variability.

results.result: The type 1 pilus rod structure was determined at 4.2 Å resolution using cryo-EM from type 1 pili present as contaminants in a T4P preparation. The structure reveals a 70 Å diameter helical rod with 115° rotation and 7.7 Å translation per subunit, where each FimA subunit interacts with six adjacent subunits through donor strand complementation.
results.evaluation: The cryo-EM structure determination is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including FSC plots (C1), detailed image processing parameters (C135-C138), confirmation of sample identity by sequencing (C132), and structural measurements (C2-C4, C70-C73). The resolution estimate is validated by map quality features and the ability to build an atomic model without ambiguities.

results.result: Donor strand complementation in the type 1 pilus involves predominantly hydrophobic interactions, with Val5, Val10, and Phe12 from the N-terminal β-strand inserting into a hydrophobic groove of the adjacent subunit. The structure reveals conformational flexibility in residues 22-33 that differs from previously solved crystal structures.
results.evaluation: The structural details of donor strand complementation are directly observed in the cryo-EM density (C5, C6, C73) and are supported by comparison with crystal structures (C74). The identification of conformational differences in residues 22-33 (C75, C76) and the inference about functional necessity (C77) are well-justified by the structural data.

results.result: Sequence analysis of 1,828 FimA proteins reveals that 83.9% of residues are highly conserved, with FimA being significantly more variable than other type 1 pilus components (FimC and FimH). Non-conserved residues are located exclusively on the exterior surface, while residues at subunit interfaces and lining the lumen are 100% conserved.
results.evaluation: The sequence conservation analysis is based on a large dataset (C7, C8) with appropriate comparative analysis (C9). The mapping of conservation onto the structure (C10-C12) provides strong support for the functional interpretation. The comparison with other E. coli genes (C85) and differences between FimA variants (C91) are well-documented.

results.result: Evolutionary analysis reveals that 66 codons in fimA are under purifying selection while 5 codons show adaptive selection. All positively selected sites are located on the exterior surface away from subunit interfaces, indicating evolutionary pressure to conserve structural residues while diversifying surface-exposed residues.
results.evaluation: The dN/dS analysis is appropriately conducted on 191 unique sequences (C13, C14) with proper accounting for recombination. The mapping of selection pressure onto structure (C15, C94) provides strong support for the interpretation. The conclusion about evolutionary pressures (C96, C97) is well-justified by the combined sequence and structural data.

results.result: The fimA gene is carried by 96.3% of UPEC strains analyzed, but there is no single FimA variant found in all UPEC strains. Three branches in the phylogeny show statistically significant episodic diversifying selection, including branches carrying most clinical UPEC strains.
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic analysis is based on a curated dataset of 67 E. coli genomes (C16) with appropriate statistical testing for episodic selection (C17). The observation that UPEC strains are distributed throughout the phylogeny (C95) is directly supported by the phylogenetic tree data.

results.result: Five FimA mutations (A25R, V32R, V65R, V85R, P145R) abolished pilus assembly, and these mutations occur at residues under strong purifying selection or too conserved for evolutionary analysis, suggesting they disrupt critical interactions with FimC/FimD or proper folding.
results.evaluation: The hemagglutination assays demonstrate loss of pilus function (C18), and the correlation with evolutionary conservation (C99, C100) provides strong support for the functional importance. The inference about mechanism (C98) is reasonable given the conservation patterns and structural context.

results.result: Expression of FimA mutants V5R, E45R, E121R, A142R, D62R, and D114R resulted in bacterial clumping, with mutations occurring at residues showing variable levels of conservation and purifying selection. The clumping phenotype is associated with mutations in codons under different selective pressures.
results.evaluation: The clumping phenotype is directly observed (C19, C101) and the correlation with sequence conservation is documented (C102, C103). The analysis of selection pressure on clumping-associated mutations (C62) provides insight into evolutionary constraints, though the mechanistic interpretation (C54) remains speculative.

results.result: Optical tweezers measurements reveal that wild-type type 1 pili unwind at 30.3 ± 0.2 pN, while all tested FimA mutants show reduced unwinding force. The A22R variant shows the largest reduction (11.2 ± 0.2 pN), consistent with structural analysis showing Ala22 is tightly packed against residues from other subunits.
results.evaluation: The optical tweezers measurements are well-controlled with appropriate replication (C20-C22) and the values are consistent with literature (C50). The structural explanation for the A22R phenotype (C23, C51) is well-supported by the cryo-EM model. The interpretation of the unwinding mechanism (C104-C106) is reasonable based on established understanding.

results.result: In competitive and single-strain chronic bladder infection experiments, FimA variants D62R, D114R, and A22R were significantly attenuated compared to wild-type, while P132R showed no defect. The A22R variant was completely unable to establish chronic infection, with 100% of mice resolving infection.
results.evaluation: The chronic infection experiments are well-designed with appropriate controls and replication (C24-C28). The competitive index data and single-strain infection rates provide convergent evidence for attenuation. The inference that chronic defects are due to acute deficiencies (C111) is reasonable given the temporal data.

results.result: FimA variants A22R and D114R significantly impaired IBC formation at 6 hours post-infection, with 70% of A22R-infected mice forming no IBCs. The A22R mutant was severely attenuated in bladder cell invasion starting at 1 hour post-infection.
results.evaluation: The IBC enumeration data (C29-C31) and invasion assays (C32) provide direct evidence for acute infection defects. The experiments include appropriate time points and controls, with clear quantitative differences between mutants and wild-type.

results.result: FimA variants D62R, D114R, and A22R showed 2-log reductions in intestinal colonization compared to wild-type, mirroring defects seen in fim deletion strains. The P132R variant showed a non-significant 1-log reduction. Overall, gut colonization defects were less severe than bladder infection defects.
results.evaluation: The intestinal colonization experiments are appropriately designed with streptomycin pretreatment (C33). The comparison with deletion mutants (C34) provides context for the magnitude of the defect. The observation about differential severity (C127) is supported by direct comparison of the data, though the P132R result lacks statistical significance (C118).

results.result: All FimA mutant strains with chromosomal mutations demonstrated similar levels of hemagglutination compared to wild-type despite some variability in piliation levels, indicating that the mutations do not prevent expression or function of type 1 pili in vitro.
results.evaluation: The hemagglutination assays (C107) and EM analysis of piliation (C108) provide direct evidence that pili are functional in vitro. The correlation between mannose-resistant hemagglutination and clumping (C109) is an interesting observation. The conclusion (C110) is well-supported by the in vitro characterization data.

results.result: The D62R variant showed defects in chronic but not acute bladder infection, forming similar numbers of IBCs as wild-type at 6 hpi but showing delayed bacterial clearance starting between 10-14 days post-infection.
results.evaluation: The temporal analysis of D62R infection (C112-C115) reveals a distinct phenotype from other mutants, with normal early infection but delayed clearance. The IBC data (C113) and longitudinal urinalysis (C115) provide strong support for a late-stage defect.

results.result: Integration of evolutionary and functional analyses reveals that mutations preventing pilus assembly occur at codons under strong purifying selection, while many codons under purifying selection maintain the force required to unwind the pilus rod, suggesting a 'weak' rod is as detrimental as no rod.
results.evaluation: The integration of evolutionary analysis with functional data (C63, C65) provides novel insights into selective pressures. The inference about differential harm (C64, C66) is well-reasoned based on the patterns of selection associated with different phenotypes.

results.result: The mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod are essential for mediating E. coli pathogenesis and persistence in both bladder and gut, and these properties appear to have been evolutionarily tuned. The FimA sequence is critical for pilus function and has a major impact on UTI outcomes.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion (C67, C68, C119, C120) is well-supported by the integration of structural, biophysical, evolutionary, and in vivo data. The multiple lines of evidence from different experimental approaches provide strong support for the central thesis.

results.result: Comparison with previous NMR models and P pilus structure reveals significant differences in subunit packing and N-terminal organization. The type 1 pilus N-terminus projects outward making no contacts, while the P pilus N-terminus forms a 'staple' contacting multiple subunits.
results.evaluation: The structural comparisons are quantitative (C80, C81) and highlight important differences between models and between pilus types (C82, C83). These comparisons provide validation for the current structure and reveal functional differences between pilus types.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that the A22R mutant pilus lacks sufficient strength to withstand shear forces during urination, leading to bacterial clearance. Alternative mechanisms including protease exposure are considered but not excluded.
results.evaluation: These claims are explicitly speculative (C125, C126, C128, C52, C56, C57) and represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, no direct evidence for the shear force mechanism or protease exposure is provided.

results.result: The 100% conservation of lumen-lining residues is likely due to their involvement in subunit-subunit contacts rather than transport function, as every lumen residue either makes contacts or is packed between contact-making residues.
results.evaluation: The structural analysis of lumen residues (C90) provides a more parsimonious explanation than transport (C89). The claim is supported by detailed examination of residue positions and interactions in the structure.

results.result: The study demonstrates that cryo-EM can successfully determine near-atomic resolution structures from contaminating filaments in heterogeneous preparations, overcoming the crystallographic challenges of helical polymers that lack crystallographically favorable symmetry.
results.evaluation: The methodological achievement is well-documented (C121-C123, C130) and the explanation of crystallographic limitations (C129) is accurate. This represents an important technical advance in structural biology methodology.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on type 1 pili, UPEC pathogenesis, CUP pili diversity, and UTI epidemiology, citing established literature and identifying knowledge gaps regarding FimA immune recognition.
results.evaluation: These claims represent well-established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature (C35-C49, C53, C58-C60, C69, C116, C117). The identification of knowledge gaps (C61) is accurate and motivates the study.
